overview:
Cambodia lies in the heart of mainland Southeast Asia, bordered by Thailand, Laos and Vietnam, with a short coast on the Gulf of Thailand. It is about 181,000 km², roughly the size of the US state of Missouri, and home to about 17 million people. The capital, Phnom Penh, sits where the Mekong River meets the Tonlé Sap River.

Almost everyone speaks Khmer, a language with its own curvy alphabet, and most people are Buddhists. Cambodia's greatest treasure is Angkor, the ancient capital near Siem Reap, whose temples include Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world. The temple's five towers appear on the national flag, one of the few flags to show a building.

Cambodia is a constitutional monarchy with a king and an elected government, though one party has held power for decades. Most Cambodians farm rice or fish, and clothing factories and tourism have grown quickly. The country is still recovering from the 1970s, when the Khmer Rouge regime killed roughly a quarter of its people.
landAndNature:
Cambodia is a wide, low bowl of rice fields surrounded by hills: the Cardamom and Elephant Mountains to the southwest and the Dangrek range along the Thai border. The Mekong, one of the world's great rivers, flows through the country from north to south. Every monsoon season it swells so much that the Tonlé Sap River reverses direction and flows backward into the Tonlé Sap lake, which grows to about five times its dry-season size.

That flooding makes the lake one of the richest freshwater fisheries on Earth, with whole villages of floating houses moving with the water. The climate is hot year-round, wet from May to October. Rare Irrawaddy dolphins live in the Mekong, and the forests shelter Asian elephants, sun bears, gibbons and the giant ibis, the national bird.
peopleAndCulture:
Khmer people make up about 95 percent of the population, with Cham, Vietnamese and Chinese minorities. Buddhism shapes daily life; boys often spend time as monks, and saffron-robed monks collect food each morning. Cambodians greet each other with the sampeah, palms pressed together with a bow.

Fish is the key food, especially prahok, a strong fermented fish paste, and fish amok, a creamy coconut curry steamed in banana leaves. Breakfast is often noodle soup. The graceful Apsara dance, with slow hand movements copied from temple carvings, nearly died out in the 1970s and was revived. Kun Khmer kickboxing is the traditional sport, and soccer is popular. Khmer New Year in April means water fights and games, while the Water Festival in November brings colorful boat races to Phnom Penh.
history:
Early kingdoms called Funan and Chenla traded with India and China, bringing Hinduism and Buddhism to the region. In 802 Jayavarman II founded the Khmer Empire, which ruled much of Southeast Asia for 600 years from Angkor, a city of canals and temples that may have held nearly a million people, the largest in the world before modern times. Angkor Wat was built in the 1100s.

The empire faded after 1431, and Cambodia was squeezed by Thailand and Vietnam until France made it a protectorate in 1863. Independence came in 1953 under King Norodom Sihanouk. The Vietnam War spilled across the border, and in 1975 the Khmer Rouge under Pol Pot seized power, emptying cities and forcing people into labor camps; about two million died from execution, starvation and disease. Vietnam ousted the regime in 1979, and United Nations-backed elections in 1993 restored the monarchy.
funFacts: Angkor Wat covers about 160 hectares and is the largest religious building on Earth, bigger than Vatican City.
Most Hindu temples face east, but Angkor Wat faces west, which some scholars think means it was built as a tomb.
Laser scans from aircraft revealed that medieval Angkor spread over an area the size of a modern city like Los Angeles.
The Tonlé Sap is the only major river in the world that reverses its flow every year.
Cambodians use two currencies every day: the riel for small purchases and US dollars for larger ones.
Kampot pepper, grown near the coast, is so prized that chefs around the world pay premium prices for it.
